newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha says Socialists delay Albanian poll result.
newsitem.headline: Berisha says Socialists delay Albanian poll result.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha on Thursday accused the Socialists of whipping up a climate of terror to help them win last month's elections but denied he was holding up the final results.
He told reporters he wanted to convene the new parliament as soon as possible and would then step down.

Media reports said the electoral commission had not announced the results of the June 29 election and subsequent run-offs because of a dispute over whether to include Berisha among the list of deputies elected.
"In the last two days, the propaganda of the election winners has been making a big noise about the alleged delay caused by the president of the republic in convening parliament," Berisha said.
He said he had been elected president by a legitimate parliament which was the product of a more free and fair vote than its successor.

Berisha said he recognised the victory of the reformed communist Socialists and their coalition allies, "although the victory as it is clear to Albanians and international opinion has its roots in violence, terror, assassination attempts and killings, organised by the victors before and during the election campaign.
"Its roots lie also in cheating to create special sources to pay back and compensate the money lost in the collapse of pyramid schemes plus its interest in full," Berisha said.
"I believe it will very soon dwindle through the powerful winds of democracy."

Election monitors from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said the election, in which Berisha's Democrats suffered a resounding defeat, had been acceptable, if far from perfect.
The vote was called in March after the collapse of pyramid savings funds triggered a violent rebellion that led to more than 1,500 deaths, prompting Berisha's government to resign.

With all but two seats declared, the electoral commission said last week the Socialists had 99 seats in the 153-seat parliament, plus another 15 held by their coalition allies, giving them the two thirds majority needed for major legislative changes. Berisha's Democratic Party had 29.

The daily Koha Jone on Thursday quoted interim prime minister Bashkim Fino as saying he was playing soccer every afternoon to show Berisha he had nothing to do and was waiting for him to convene parliament.

Berisha said he had received a letter on Tuesday signed by two Socialist members of the commission asking him to clarify whether he planned to remain president or take up his mandate as a deputy, then a second letter from the commission saying the first document represented only those members' personal position.

"I want to confirm to you once again that I am totally determined to decree the convening of parliament and that the delay by the Socialist leadership marks another stage of their revenge towards state institutions after the decision, which it looks like they have cancelled, to invest the prime minister with presidential powers and to create an honorific president," Berisha said.

"Upon fulfilling my important constitutional obligations, I will hand in my resignation, will not cohabit with the government that will come out of the new elections, and am determined as soon as the final election results are made public to decree the convening of parliament at the earliest date."
